comparison.objective: Candidate commissions and locks a robot-axis shock absorber through iterative physical impact testing; PR-1411 finishes an electrical splice by evening wire tips and twisting on a wire connector. These are meaningfully different outcomes.
comparison.physical_skill: Candidate requires recessed hex-key engagement, captive-set-screw loosening/relocking, collar regrasping, bimanual stabilization, bounded tightening, and adjustment based on dynamic stopping response. PR-1411 requires aligning flexible wire ends and twisting a wire nut until snug. They share only generic alignment and rotation primitives.
comparison.success_condition: Candidate requires two repeatable, physically simulated carriage stops within stroke, energy, velocity, rebound, overload, hard-stop, and post-lock drift limits, with unsafe or state-written shortcuts rejected. PR-1411 succeeds when wire tips are even and the connector is twisted clockwise until snug. Its available record has no spec versions, numeric snugness threshold, damage criteria, or detailed scoring rubric, but those omissions do not make this clearly unrelated objective a plausible duplicate.
comparison.reason: The tested ability and measured outcome differ substantially: dynamic damper tuning and retention under repeated impacts versus forming a mechanically secure wire splice. Similar hand motions do not establish task overlap.
